newsitem.title: USA: Lucent fills messaging gap with Octel deal.
newsitem.headline: Lucent fills messaging gap with Octel deal.

text.p: Lucent Technologies Inc's $1.8 billion plan to acquire voice-messaging leader Octel Communications Corp is a temporary setback for its high-flying stock but should turn into a boon by giving Lucent a big stake in a fast growing business.
"This makes imminent sense. It think it is a fair price for Lucent, and a good price for Octel shareholders," said Salomon Bros analyst Steve Levy of the $31-per-share deal.
The total messaging market is currently worth more than $5 billion annually and is expected to double to by 2000, Lucent said in the statement announcing the deal.
In afternoon trade, Lucent stock tumbled 3.2 percent, or 2-13/16, to 86-7/8 while Octel shares rose 13.1 percent, or 3-1/2, to 30-1/4.
Lucent shares have been a Wall Street favorite during the current bull market, soaring from the initial public offering price of $27 in April 1996 when the company was spun off from AT&T Corp.
But the stock's battering today was due to an unspecified charge Lucent said it will take to write-off Octel's research and development, traders said.
The charge will be taken in Lucent's fiscal fourth quarter ending in September, and will have a "significant" impact on the company's earnings for the quarter and 1997 fiscal year.
The company declined to provide more detail on the charge.
Lucent, based in Murray Hill, N.J., reported yesterday fiscal third quarter revenues of $6.34 billion and earnings of $213 million, or $0.33 per share.
Octel, based in Milpitas, Calif. reported in April fiscal third quarter revenues of $150.2 million and earnings of $10.6 million, or $0.20 per share.
"Lucent is looking to grow its business in high-growth areas like voice processing, which is growing at 20 percent a year," said Lehman Bros telecom equipment analyst Tim Luke.

"The (messaging) business is so strong because there is good demand for network service operators, wireless and wireline, to put in voice messaging. In the extreme, there should be a voice-mailbox on every line, so you always have a completed call," said Levy.

With messaging, "There is never a busy never, never a ring-no-answer. If you complete a call you get revenues, and if the call results in a voice message, the chances are the message will be returned, which is more revenues," Levy said.
In a conference call with reporters, the president of Lucent's business communications systems unit, Bill O'Shea, emphasized the pro-growth strategy of the acqusition.
"This deal is all about sustainable growth from expanding our core businesses. The messaging business is growing at about 20 percent per year. We see a superior fit," he said.
"Don't expect that this is going to be the final thing you hear about investing (by Lucent)," O'Shea added.
He declined to specify what areas of the company may be affected by future transactions.
With Octel, Lucent also will add significantly to its international messaging presense with Octel's customer base that includes more than 140 (telephone) service providers in 40 countries.
